binders: q(x,t) denotes the state as a function of spatial position x and time t; its components represent densities of conserved quantities. The component count is not specified in this passage. [Printed p. 4, opening paragraph and Section 1.1.1, explanation after (1.10).]
f is the physical flux function evaluated on q. The surrounding discussion allows nonlinear flux functions and mentions the linear example f(q)=Aq. [Printed p. 4, opening paragraph and (1.10).]

x₁ and x₂ are arbitrary spatial endpoints: the source explicitly says 'for any two points'. No explicit time interval or endpoint-order restriction is supplied. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, introduction to (1.10).]

Grid cells and successive time steps are the numerical objects in the selected paragraph; no cell-index set, mesh parameters, or quantified time-step range is introduced there. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]
hypotheses: The conservation setting has changes in the total amount accounted for only by boundary fluxes; processes that do not conserve the quantity require source terms beyond the displayed balance. [Printed p. 4, paragraph after (1.10).]

The domain is divided into grid cells, and the numerical data consist of approximate cell averages. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph, 'break the domain into grid cells' and 'the only data available'.]

Sufficient smoothness of q and f(q) is a condition for deriving the classical differential equation from the integral equation; it is not presented as a condition restricting finite volume methods to smooth solutions. [Printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2; printed p. 5, Section 1.2, opening sentences.]
conclusions: The continuum balance is d/dt ∫[x₁,x₂] q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)): the first endpoint flux enters with a plus sign and the second with a minus sign. [Printed p. 4, equation (1.10).]
Finite volume methods approximate cell integrals or cell averages and modify these quantities at each time step through cell-edge fluxes. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]

The numerical task is to construct flux functions that approximate the correct fluxes reasonably well from the available approximate cell averages. This is a methodological requirement, without a quantitative error conclusion in the passage. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph, sentence beginning 'These values are modified'.]

The integral conservation formulation continues to apply at discontinuities, where the differential equation does not hold in the classical sense. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2, paragraph beginning 'At a discontinuity'.]
definitions_and_conventions: A cell average is the integral of q over the cell divided by the volume of that cell. The integral and average therefore have distinct normalization. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]

The phrase 'total mass' refers to the total amount of the conserved quantity represented by a component of q, rather than exclusively physical mass. [Printed p. 4, explanation immediately after (1.10).]

Physical flux is denoted f(q); numerical flux functions approximate the correct fluxes using approximate cell averages. No formula identifying these two types of flux is given. [Printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]
implicit_context: The displayed inherited conservation equation uses one spatial coordinate and two endpoints; the numerical description uses the terms cell volume and cell edges without specifying a mesh geometry. [Printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]
Discontinuous solutions, including shock waves, motivate the use of the integral formulation; discontinuities may develop from smooth initial data. [Printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2.]

The following subsection provides a possible construction using neighboring cell averages Q_{i−1} and Q_i as Riemann initial states. It says the resulting information can be used for a numerical flux, without making that construction a universal requirement on every method described in Section 1.2. contract_plain_english: Finite volume methods divide the domain into cells and approximate the amount of a conserved quantity in each cell, usually expressed as its cell average: the integral divided by cell volume. Each time step changes these quantities through cell-edge fluxes, with numerical flux functions constructed from the available approximate cell averages to approximate the correct fluxes reasonably well. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.] The inherited continuum balance identifies the rate of change of the integral between two endpoints with the first endpoint's physical flux minus the second endpoint's physical flux. [Printed p. 4, equation (1.10) and its explanation.] The integral formulation remains applicable at discontinuities, unlike the classical differential equation. [Printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2.] The selected passage does not uniquely specify a discrete recurrence, flux normalization, stencil, or quantitative accuracy guarantee. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph.]
